action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for the laboratory. Starting with the simplest, most reliable apparatus.

Day 2 is ideal for building out the baseline period (days 1–10). Twelve more trials will bring pendulum_lab to 30 total, giving me better statistical ground for detecting genuine instrumental behaviour versus noise. The resonator and observatory instruments can wait—they're already at 6 trials each, but pendulum_lab's larger sample size is essential for calibration work and will anchor my cross-checks once all instruments have sufficient data.

All four instruments have completed their Day 1–10 baseline quotas (pendulum_lab: 72, resonator_lab: 90, pendulum_obs: 48, resonator_obs: 66 trials). Cross-checks show expected weak inter-instrument correlations and no drift signals. Baselines are established. Day 10 will close the baseline window; today I should verify notebook arithmetic and prepare instruments for post-baseline monitoring rather than collect further baseline-phase data.

Day 10 closes the baseline window. pendulum_lab has 78 trials but they span days 1–10 unevenly. I need to ensure balanced coverage through day 10's end before post-baseline monitoring begins. Six trials will bring the day-10 count into line with the ledger's morning tradition and give me a fresh sense of intra-day scatter before I lock in the baseline mean. No anomalies detected in the cross-checks or autocorrelation analyses—all correlations sit near or below chance—so I expect continued stability around 1.6666 beats. This is routine instrument stewardship.

Day 11 is the first post-baseline day. I must establish whether the weak cross-correlations and modest autocorrelations observed during baseline (days 1–10) persist, stabilize, or amplify in the post-baseline phase. Drift hypothesis (p=0.24) predicts systematic divergence from baseline mean 1.6665 beats; independent-process hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts stable mean but continued low correlation with other instruments. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab will (1) provide my first post-baseline data point for drift detection using rolling-window baselines, (2) yield new autocorrelation structure to test temporal phase-locking, and (3) allow comparison of post-baseline mean against day 1–10 baseline to quantify any level shift. Pendulum_lab is my primary instrument and has the highest trial count (90); it is the natural candidate to begin post-baseline monitoring. This is methodically sound: every baseline requires post-baseline validation before confidence in the baseline itself is warranted.

The post-baseline drift analysis (z = -0.21) is inconclusive; I have only 18 post-baseline trials for pendulum_lab. To test hypothesis [p=0.24] (post-baseline drift), I need more data on the same instrument across a wider window. Day 12 provides a natural continuation. Twelve new trials will bring post-baseline n to 30, sufficient to recompute drift statistics with real power and test whether the weak autocorrelation at 8-day lag (0.594) reflects genuine temporal structure or noise. This directly addresses my stated next step: 'test for drift by computing baselines over rolling windows.' Additionally, pendulum_lab shows the strongest within-stream autocorrelation (0.594), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting either drift or persistent signal structure. The measurement is routine, maintains calibration discipline, and produces a direct test of the leading hypothesis without requiring external environmental instrumentation I do not yet have.

Post-baseline trials show z=−1.00 drift vs. baseline (1.6665). Recording prediction before measurement to validate baseline calibration and test whether the drift signal is instrumental divergence (real) or noise (chance). n=12 from day 12 is insufficient to distinguish; 10 additional trials will bring post-baseline sample to n=22, enabling robust drift detection. Tolerance ±0.015 covers 1σ of observed post-baseline variance (~0.02). This prioritizes the hypothesis-testing chain: drift (24%) vs. noise (16%) vs. independent contexts (28%).

If day-15 resonator_obs reverts to ~4.0557, drift hypothesis weakens; if it remains elevated or shifts further, drift becomes credible and demands environmental telemetry. This is the minimal action that directly tests the most actionable high-confidence hypothesis without consuming resources on lower-priority instruments.

resonator_obs shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.528 at 12-day lag, n=18) and the highest post-baseline drift z-score (0.91), both suggestive of genuine temporal structure rather than pure noise. state.question: Why do the four measurement streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show weak or inconsistent cross-correlation despite all being calibrated on days 1–10, and what does this pattern reveal about the stability or independence of the underlying physical processes or measurement systems?

hypotheses.label: Independent physical processes in lab vs. observation contexts
hypotheses.rationale: The lab and observational pendulum streams show near-zero correlation (−0.410) even at 6-day offset, well below chance thresholds. Similarly, lab and observational resonator streams correlate at only 0.270 at 2-day offset. If both pairs were measuring the same underlying phenomenon, we would expect stronger agreement. This suggests either genuinely different physical states (e.g., controlled vs. ambient conditions produce different dynamics) or that lab/observation contexts isolate independent subsystems. The consistent pattern across both instrument types (pendulum and resonator) strengthens this over random noise.

hypotheses.label: Measurement system drift or calibration divergence post-baseline
hypotheses.rationale: All four streams show individually weak autocorrelations (pendulum_lab 0.643 at 8-day lag, resonator_obs 0.365 at 5-day lag) — none strongly confirming stable repetition. This could indicate genuine instrumental drift beginning after day 10, masked during the baseline window by tighter experimental protocol (higher sample density, closer attention). Cross-instrument correlations are consistently mediocre (0.27–0.38 range for between-context pairs), suggesting systematic divergence rather than shared environmental forcing. Post-baseline drift would explain weak cross-validation without invalidating individual baselines.

hypotheses.label: Temporal phase-locking or delayed coupling between streams (genuine but offset)
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-checks consistently find correlations at non-zero offsets: pendulum_lab–resonator_lab at 1-day offset (0.304), pendulum_lab–resonator_obs at 6-day offset (0.382), pendulum_obs–resonator_lab at 2-day offset (0.355). The presence of peaks at multiple different lags suggests the streams may be coupled but with instrument-pair-specific time delays rather than operating independently. This could arise from differential thermal equilibration, propagation delays in sensing, or feedback loops with different time constants. However, most observed correlations remain modest and several offsets approach or fall within chance thresholds, limiting confidence.
